items: Save your emergency vet's direct number in your phone and post it on the refrigerator — you need to reach someone immediately if warning signs appear, not navigate a voicemail tree when every hour matters.
Monitor your cat's urine output every 12 hours during the first 48 hours at home — no urine production for 12 or more hours is a re-blockage emergency requiring immediate veterinary contact.
Watch for repeated hard straining with zero urine output combined with a hard, distended belly — this combination indicates the bladder has re-blocked and requires immediate emergency care.

Log your cat's behavior, appetite, and litter box visits for the first week after coming home — this creates a personal baseline so you can spot problems before they become life-threatening emergencies.

Create a medication tracking chart listing every prescription name, dosage, administration time, and end date — administer every dose on schedule without skipping, because missed anti-inflammatory or muscle relaxant doses can trigger dangerous inflammation rebound.

Set up at least 2 litter boxes in the quietest area of your home using unscented clumping litter — each box must have a low entry lip of 2 inches or less so your sore cat can access it without avoiding the box due to discomfort.

Keep your recovering cat separated from other cats in a quiet room during the first week — your cat does not need to defend territory or feel threatened while healing, and gradual reintroduction through door-sniffing can begin after several days.

Switch to wet prescription food at every meal instead of feeding dry food — higher moisture content produces more dilute urine, which reduces crystal concentration and significantly lowers blockage recurrence risk.

Place multiple water stations throughout your home or add a flowing water fountain — cats drink more when water is fresh-tasting and available in several locations, which directly increases urine dilution.
Weigh your cat on the same scale weekly and record the results — obesity increases blockage recurrence risk, and tracking weight monthly lets you adjust portions before significant gain occurs.
Maintain consistent feeding times, play routines, and environmental setup long-term — stress from disrupted routines or household changes is a documented trigger for urinary issues in cats.
Check your cat's litter box daily for urine ball size, straining sounds, and blood discoloration — tracking these markers monthly lets you catch early warning signs before a full emergency develops.
